proposals.relationship: Pocock credits Bailyn, together with Caroline Robbins, with directing him toward commerce’s effects on political thought.
proposals.evidence_note: Own preface ix expressly identifies both American scholars as showing him the way through commerce before and after 1700 and 1776, then separately credits later Hont and Sonenscher work. This is a plural acknowledged scholarly debt, not formal supervision, sole derivation, or identification of a specific unread Bailyn book. The opposite existing edge_1774 records Bailyn’s use of Pocock; the reciprocal resources are not identical claims. The witness is the publisher preface in a book commonly cited as 2009, whose supplied imprint states 2008.

proposals.relationship: Pocock credits Kuhn’s paradigms with helping him think about the emergence and transformation of political languages, while limiting the analogy.
proposals.evidence_note: Own preface xi–xiii, notes 10–12, identifies The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), recalls his initial intrigue and gives the post-1688 commercial-society transformation as a useful case. He expressly recognizes an intellectual debt but calls the Kuhnian paradigm a starting point rather than an enduring universal tool. His Oakeshott debt is equally explicit and held for a missing full node. Kuhn’s original and Pocock’s full 1971 essays are unread; a later reported agreement by Kuhn is Pocock’s recollection, not independent correspondence verification.

proposals.relationship: Pocock restricts the transfer of Kuhn’s paradigm revolutions to political history because political communities sustain multiple competing languages.
proposals.evidence_note: Own preface xii–xiii distinguishes a scientific community of inquiry from political communities exposed to many problems and linguistic alternatives. He allows specific paradigm revolutions but rejects a general requirement that one framework monopolize political discussion. This is a bounded criticism of transferring the model, not a refutation of Kuhn’s account of science. Pocock describes his 1971 essay as self-criticism and says it was less a direct challenge to Kuhn than it appeared; acknowledged influence is retained.

proposals.relationship: Pocock uses Skinner’s account of what authors were doing as a starting point for tracing readers’ responses and unintended changes in political discourse.
proposals.evidence_note: Own preface xiv and note 14 explicitly credits Skinner’s 1978 formulation and borrows the language of illocution and allocution while explaining why he pressed toward what authors turned out to have done. This is an acknowledged, critically extended resource, not identical methods or exclusive derivation. The same preface ix distinguishes their research trajectories; existing opposite critique edge_1298 retains its particular 1996 state-concept objection. The Foundations original and the complete 1985 introduction remain unread.
